# Afterword: What You Built, and Where Next {.unnumbered .backmatter #sec-afterword}

Near the end of Part III, one setting changed in one script, and the officials' report, the council's
slides, the blog post and the dashboard all changed with it, without a number retyped. That moment is
what the two projects were for. The London guide and the water analysis each started from plain text
and data, became a shelf of documents for different readers, and rebuild with one command. The projects
will date. The method will not, and it fits on a card.

::: {.practice title="Prompt, Check, Publish"}
**Prompt.** Write the rules down before the first request: a short `AGENTS.md` keeps an assistant to the
project's scope, data rules and commands across sessions, and is your checklist too. Then ask for one
task at a time, naming the file, the column and the output, and ending with a check.

**Check.** Compute every number, so that it updates and can be traced back to its data. Before a
rebuild, predict what should change; afterwards, check that it did. Read every title and summary for
what it claims, and say what a result does not show.

**Publish.** Compute once, publish many: one script writes the results, and every output reads them.
Guard the sentences whose words depend on the data, so that a changed result fails the render instead
of going out wrong. Keep a known-good state, a checkpoint or a commit, so that being stuck is a short
detour.
:::

## Your own project, in three turns {.unnumbered}

The order matters more than the tools.

1. **One output, for one reader.** Start with the document your readers already ask for, usually a
   report, in a project folder with its data, kept unchanged, and an `AGENTS.md`. Prompt for the
   skeleton; check that it renders and answers the reader's question.
2. **Make it compute.** Replace every typed number with inline code that reads the data, or the results
   of one analysis script, and guard any sentence whose conclusion depends on them. Check by changing
   one input in a copy and watching the number move.
3. **Add formats, then readers.** Word or a PDF, then slides, then a website, each reading the same
   results. Check with a prediction: change a setting, say what will change, rebuild and compare. Then
   publish.

The second format is where the approach starts to repay the setup; the first change to the data is
where it pays for itself.

Assistants, models and Quarto's options will keep changing, and some details in this book with them.
The loop does not. Prompt for one thing. Check it against the data. Publish only what you checked, from
one source, as often as the data change.

## Where next {.unnumbered}

- Quarto's [Guide](https://quarto.org/docs/guide/) covers everything this book used and much it did not:
  books like this one, manuscripts, interactive documents and more output formats (checked 2026-10-30).
- [Dashboards](https://quarto.org/docs/dashboards/), [Typst](https://quarto.org/docs/output-formats/typst.html)
  and [publishing to GitHub Pages](https://quarto.org/docs/publishing/github-pages.html) are the official
  references for the three areas readers usually extend first (checked 2026-10-30).
- For the causal questions Part III left open, Miguel A. Hernán and James M. Robins,
  [*Causal Inference: What If*](https://miguelhernan.org/whatifbook) (Boca Raton: Chapman & Hall/CRC,
  2020; free online), on confounding and the designs that can answer them (checked 2026-11-12).
- In this book: @sec-cheatsheet for the commands, @sec-troubleshooting when a render fails, and
  @sec-checkpoints for every known-good state.
- The workshop's slides, examples and checkpoints are at
  <https://github.com/project-delphi/quarto-workshop>; the slides themselves are at
  <https://project-delphi.github.io/quarto-workshop/>.
